newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says flood victims in fight for lives.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says flood victims in fight for lives.

text.p: The swollen Red River threatened to rise even higher on Tuesday as residents of this flood-ravaged city, hoping for massive federal assistance, awaited a visit by President Bill Clinton.

"Welcome to Grand Forks, Mr. President. Welcome to our nightmare," the Grand Forks Herald said on its front page in advance of Clinton's arrival on Tuesday for an inspection tour of the watery region.
As he left Washington Clinton said "People are quite literally in the fight of their lives ... What they have endured is enormous. How they are enduring it is remarkable."
He vowed to "do everything we can" to help the victims and suggested "we're going to have to be prepared to be very creative" in coming up with the best way to do it.
"We hear he's going to announce a major rebuilding project up here, but we're anxiously awaiting what the news is," North Dakota Gov. Ed Schafer said.
Roughly 90 percent of this evacuated city of 50,000 was under water from the Red River, which extended its widening path of destruction northward into Canada.

Hundreds of people were evacuated from Drayton, North Dakota, 40 miles (64 km) north of Grand Forks where a cracked dike threatened to give way. Hundreds more left Pembina, and about 750 people across the border in Emerson, Manitoba, fled their homes.
The swirling, filthy floodwaters that already contain raw sewage and dissolving animal carcasses could become polluted with more than 1,000 tons of fertiliser from a storage facility near Drayton.

The slow-moving Red River reached more than 54 feet (16 metres) at Grand Forks, and could fluctuate at even higher levels on the flat, table-top landscape before receding in a few days. Residents evacuated from both sides of the river, which forms the North Dakota-Minnesota border, were told to be prepared to stay away for two weeks or longer.
Hopes centred on President Clinton, who declared the three-state plains region a disaster area two weeks ago, promising federal aid for victims of the once-in-500-years flood.
Officials said it was too early to assess the monetary costs of the slow-motion disaster until the waters recede.
The Grand Forks Herald in its article welcoming President Clinton described the flooding as "biblical."

"Even if we'd known the water was going to be this high, we might not have been able to do anything more than get out of town more quickly. And now, we're going to need our nation's help, and lots of it," the paper said.

Members of Congress representing the flooded states pleaded for massive aid, and White House officials suggested some type of "Marshall Plan" for the region, reminiscent of the programme of aid for Europe after the Second World War.
Evacuees from the flood were provided with first aid, food and beds, and the Red Cross relief organisation said it was also doling out sorely needed counselling.
"People in this area have not only been hit by the flood, but they had blizzard after blizzard," said Sue Banovetz, a Red Cross spokeswoman.

Grand Forks Mayor Pat Owens, who has praised residents and rescuers for avoiding any fatalities in the disaster, said she was unable to tell one neighbour that her home was destroyed by flood and a subsequent fire.

The fierce weekend fire above the floodwaters left a dozen buildings gutted, including the newspaper offices. Staffers moved to an elementary school and printed the paper in St. Paul from where it was shipped back by air and given away free.
"It was our town that was burning," Deputy Fire Chief Peter O'Neill told the Herald. "It doesn't seem real. You want to wake up from some dream."
Residents were thankful for a spate of warm, sunny days that was melting the last of the winter's deep snowpack.

Among the refugees at a makeshift shelter in nearby Arvilla, North Dakota, 17-year-old Kristi Brown busied herself with a puzzle and thoughts of her cancelled high school graduation. "I put my prom dress up in a closet. It should be all right -- I hope."
